text: The 2004 World Series was the championship series of Major League Baseball's (MLB) 2004 season and the 100th edition of the event, featuring a best-of-seven matchup between the American League (AL) champion Boston Red Sox and the National League (NL) champion St. Louis Cardinals. The series was played from October 23 to 27, 2004, at Fenway Park and Busch Memorial Stadium. The Red Sox swept the Cardinals in four games, securing their first World Series title since 1918 and ending the Curse of the Bambino. The Cardinals earned their playoff berth by winning the NL Central division title and finishing with the best win–loss record in the NL, while the Red Sox earned their spot via the AL wild card. The Cardinals advanced by defeating the Los Angeles Dodgers in the best-of-five NL Division Series and the Houston Astros in the best-of-seven NL Championship Series. The Red Sox defeated the Anaheim Angels in the AL Division Series and, after trailing three games to none to the New York Yankees in the AL Championship Series, came back to win the series and reach their first World Series since 1986. The Cardinals made their first World Series appearance since 1987. With the New England Patriots winning Super Bowl XXXVIII, Boston became the first city to have both a Super Bowl and World Series championship team in the same year (2004) since Pittsburgh in 1979. The Red Sox became the third consecutive wild card team to win the World Series, following the Anaheim Angels in 2002 and the Florida Marlins in 2003. The Red Sox had home-field advantage due to the AL winning the 2004 All-Star Game. In Game 1, Mark Bellhorn hit a go-ahead home run in the 8th inning, and Curt Schilling pitched six innings, allowing just one run, in Game 2. The Red Sox won the first two games despite committing four errors each. Game 3 was won by Pedro Martínez’s seven shutout innings, and in Game 4, Johnny Damon’s leadoff home run in the first inning gave the Red Sox a lead they never lost. The Cardinals did not lead in any game; the only tie occurred in the sixth and eighth innings of Game 1. Manny Ramírez was named the series' Most Valuable Player. The series was broadcast on Fox and averaged just under 25.5 million viewers. Though not particularly competitive, it is ranked among the most memorable World Series of all time and one of the most iconic moments of the 2000s due to its historical significance for Boston. The Red Sox and Cardinals met again in the 2013 World Series, which the Red Sox won 4 games to 2. This was the ninth meeting between Boston and St. Louis in a major professional sports championship, having occurred in two World Series (1946, 1967), four NBA Finals (1957, 1958, 1960, 1961), Super Bowl XXXVI two years prior, and the 1970 Stanley Cup Final. It was also the third World Series between the Red Sox and Cardinals, with the previous two (1946 and 1967) both won by the Cardinals in seven games. The Red Sox had lost in the previous season's ALCS to the Yankees, primarily due to manager Grady Little’s decision to keep Pedro Martínez in Game 7, leading to a walk-off home run by Aaron Boone off Tim Wakefield, and Little was fired two weeks later. During the off-season, the Red Sox hired Terry Francona as manager, signed Keith Foulke as closer, and traded for Curt Schilling as a starting pitcher. The Red Sox played two notable games against the Yankees during the regular season: on July 1, they came back from a 3-run deficit to force extra innings, with Yankees shortstop Derek Jeter making a catch and hurling himself head-first into the stands; the Yankees won the next inning to take an 8-game lead. On July 24, pitcher Bronson Arroyo hit Alex Rodriguez with a pitch, leading to a bench-clearing brawl after Rodriguez shouted profanities at Arroyo, with catcher Jason Varitek pushing his glove into Rodriguez’s face. The Red Sox won the game on a 9th-inning home run by Bill Mueller. On July 31, the Red Sox traded shortstop Nomar Garciaparra to the Chicago Cubs after eight years with the team, acquiring Orlando Cabrera and Doug Mientkiewicz. They won the wild card for the second consecutive year. In the AL Division Series, the Red Sox defeated the Anaheim Angels, winning Game 1 with a 7-run 4th inning and sweeping the series. In Game 3, Vladimir Guerrero hit a grand slam to tie the game, but David Ortiz won the series with a 10th-inning home run. In the ALCS, the Red Sox lost the first three games, including a 19–8 loss in Game 3, and were trailing 4–3 in Game 4 when they began the 9th inning. Kevin Millar was walked by Mariano Rivera, Dave Roberts pinch-ran and stole second, Mueller singled to tie the game, and Ortiz hit a 12th-inning home run to win 6–4. Ortiz’s single in the 14th inning of Game 5 scored the winning run, making it the longest post-season game in baseball history. Despite a dislocated ankle tendon, Schilling started Game 6 and pitched seven innings, allowing just one run, with his sock soaked in blood. In the 8th inning, Rodriguez slapped a ball out of Arroyo’s hand, allowing a run, but umpires ruled it interference and canceled the run; fans threw debris, and the game was stopped for ten minutes. The Red Sox won 4–2, becoming the first team to force a Game 7 after being down 3 games to none. A 10–3 win in Game 7 brought the Red Sox to the World Series for the first time in 18 years. The Cardinals, who were expected to finish 3rd in the NL Central, finished with the best record in the league at 105–57 due to strong offensive seasons from Albert Pujols, Scott Rolen, and Jim Edmonds—each hitting over 30 home runs and 100 RBIs—and allowing the fewest runs in the league. Four of their starters recorded at least 15 wins, and closer Jason Isringhausen had 47 saves. They added Larry Walker in August. In the NL Division Series, the Cardinals defeated the Dodgers, winning the first two games with five home runs in Game 1 and no runs allowed in Game 2; José Lima’s complete game in Game 4 forced a Game 5, which Pujols won with a home run. In the NLCS, the Cardinals won the first two games in St. Louis, tied the series in Houston, and then won Game 6 with an RBI single by Jeff Bagwell and a walk-off home run by Edmonds in the 12th inning. In Game 7, trailing in the 6th, Pujols hit a game-tying RBI double, Rolen hit a two-run home run, and Walker hit an RBI single in the 8th to give the Cardinals a 5–2 win and their first World Series berth in 17 years. Tony La Russa became the sixth manager to win pennants in both leagues after leading the Oakland Athletics to three straight pennants from 1988 to 1990 and winning the 1989 World Series; he wore #10 in tribute to Sparky Anderson and to indicate he was trying to win the team’s 10th championship. Media analysis predicted the Cardinals would win in seven games, with Andrew Haskett noting that Chris Carpenter was injured and the Red Sox had the edge in defense and key hitters like Ortiz and Pujols, Rolen, and Edmonds, concluding the Red Sox would win. John Donovan of Sports Illustrated called the series a "blast from the past" and noted the Red Sox had the edge in pitching and the Cardinals in defense and batting, predicting a Red Sox win in six games. Jim Molony of MLB.com expected a different outcome than in 1967, when both teams had strong offenses and dominant pitching. Dan Shaughnessy of The Boston Globe stated that Bally's in Las Vegas had the Red Sox as 8–5 favorites and noted some sentiment in St. Louis that the NL champions were disrespected, but Red Sox GM Theo Epstein did not want to disrespect the Cardinals. Shaughnessy quoted Schilling as saying, "There's a lot of good players in that [visitors] clubhouse over there. This isn't the time for us to be thinking about history. If we get three wins and 26 outs into the fourth win, I'm pretty sure it will hit us," and emphasized that winning the series was the only way to end the Curse of the Bambino, which he had publicized in 1990, and that chants of "1918!" would no longer echo at Yankee Stadium. Both teams had previously lost in seven-game World Series appearances: the Red Sox lost to the Mets in 1986, and the Cardinals lost to the Twins in 1987. When they met in 1946 and 1967, the Cardinals won both in seven games. With the AL winning the All-Star Game, the Red Sox had home-field advantage at Fenway Park in four of the seven games. Boston won the series 4–0. Before Game 1, local band Dropkick Murphys performed "Tessie," and a moment of silence was observed to remember student Victoria Snelgrove, who had been killed by police two days earlier as fans celebrated the AL pennant. Steven Tyler of Aerosmith performed "The Star-Spangled Banner," and Red Sox legend Carl Yastrzemski threw the ceremonial first pitch. Kelly Clarkson sang "God Bless America" during the seventh-inning stretch. In Game 1, Ortiz hit a three-run home run in his first-ever World Series at-bat, and Kevin Millar scored on a single by Bill Mueller, giving the Red Sox a 4–0 lead. The Cardinals scored one run in the second on a sacrifice fly by Mike Matheny to score Jim Edmonds and one in the third on a solo home run by Walker. In the bottom of the third, the Red Sox scored three runs after seven consecutive batters reached base, giving them a five-run lead. Dan Haren replaced Williams in the inning. In the top of the fourth, Bronson Arroyo replaced Wakefield after four walks, and errors by Millar and Doug Mirabelli, along with a passed ball, reduced the lead to two. So Taguchi reached first on an infield hit and advanced to second when Arroyo threw the ball into the stands. Doubles by Édgar Rentería and Walker tied the game at seven. In the bottom of the seventh, Ramírez singled with two men on base, and a poor throw by Edmonds allowed Mark Bellhorn to score. Ortiz hit a line drive that skipped off the infield lip and hit Cardinals’ second baseman Tony Womack with "considerable force," who immediately grabbed his clavicle and was replaced by Marlon Anderson; a precautionary X-ray revealed no damage. In the top of the eighth, with one out and two men on base, closer Keith Foulke came in. Rentería singled toward Ramírez, who unintentionally kicked the ball away, allowing Jason Marquis to score. Walker hit the ball toward Ramírez, who slid in to try to catch it, tripped and deflected the ball, and the fourth Red Sox error of the game occurred, with Roger Cedeño scoring to tie the game at nine. In the bottom of the eighth, Jason Varitek reached on an error, and Bellhorn hit a home run off the right field foul pole (Pesky's Pole) for his third home run in three games, giving the Red Sox a two-run lead. In the ninth, Foulke struck out Cedeño to win the game 11–9. The game had 20 runs, the highest-scoring opening game in World Series history. Ortiz recorded four RBI, tying a franchise record for RBI in a World Series game. Walker, making his World Series debut in Game 1, collected four hits in five at-bats with a home run and two doubles, tying a Cardinals World Series record and becoming the first to do so since Lou Brock.

In Game 1, the Red Sox committed four fielding errors, including two by Roger Cedeño, who scored on a play to tie the game at nine. In the bottom of the eighth, Jason Varitek reached on an error, and Bellhorn hit a home run off the right field foul pole, also known as Pesky's Pole, for his third home run in three games, giving the Red Sox a two-run lead. In the ninth, Foulke struck out Cedeño to win the game 11–9. The game featured 20 runs, the highest-scoring opening game of a World Series ever. With four RBI, Ortiz tied a franchise record for RBI in a World Series game. Walker, making his World Series debut in Game 1, collected four hits in five at-bats with a home run and two doubles, tying a Cardinals World Series record and becoming the seventh overall and first since Lou Brock in 1967, also against Boston. Before Game 2, Boston native James Taylor performed "The Star-Spangled Banner" and Donna Summer, also a Boston native, performed "God Bless America" during the seventh-inning stretch. The ceremonial first pitch was thrown by surviving members of the 1946 Red Sox quartet: Bobby Doerr, Dom DiMaggio, and Johnny Pesky (Ted Williams had died two years earlier). Despite a torn tendon in his right ankle, similar to Game 6 of the ALCS against the Yankees, Schilling started Game 2, having four stitches in the ankle the day before and experiencing considerable discomfort; after one stitch was removed, he was treated with antibiotics and pitched. Morris started for the Cardinals on three days' rest (one day fewer than orthodox). In the first inning, Albert Pujols doubled with two out, and Scott Rolen hit a line drive to Mueller, who caught it to end the inning. Morris walked Ramírez and Ortiz, and Varitek tripled to center to give the Red Sox a 2–0 lead. In the fourth, Pujols doubled again and scored on an error by Mueller. Bellhorn doubled with two runners on base, giving the Red Sox a three-run lead. Cal Eldred replaced Morris in the fifth after he walked the leadoff hitter and had given up four runs in the previous four innings. Mueller committed his World Series record-tying third error in the sixth. In the bottom of the sixth, Trot Nixon led off with a single, and two more singles by Johnny Damon and Orlando Cabrera enabled two more runs to score, making it 6–1. Schilling allowed no earned runs in six innings, totaling 13 innings against the Yankees and Cardinals with only one earned run allowed on a torn ankle tendon. Alan Embree pitched a scoreless seventh, Mike Timlin replaced him in the eighth, and a sacrifice fly by Scott Rolen reduced the Red Sox lead to four. Keith Foulke struck out Jim Edmonds to end the inning and pitched the ninth to secure the win, making it the second game in a row the Red Sox won despite four fielding errors. Schilling became only the fifth pitcher to win a World Series game with a team from both leagues, previously doing so with the Philadelphia Phillies in 1993 and the Arizona Diamondbacks in 2001. He later donated the bloody sock he wore to the Baseball Hall of Fame museum. Much of the blame for the Cardinals' losses in the first two games was directed at Rolen, Edmonds, and Reggie Sanders, who combined for one hit in 22 at-bats. Seattle Mariners designated hitter Edgar Martínez received the 2004 Roberto Clemente Award after announcing his retirement one month prior. The ceremonial first pitch was thrown by Stan Musial and caught by Bob Gibson. "The Star-Spangled Banner" and "God Bless America" were sung by Martina McBride and Amy Grant. A 12 by 12 foot (3.7 m × 3.7 m) Taco Bell sign, reading "Free Taco Here," was hung 420 feet (130 m) from home plate over the left-center field bullpen, with Taco Bell promising a free "Crunchy Beef Taco" to everyone in the U.S. if hit. In Game 2, the Red Sox took the lead in the first inning when Ramírez hit a home run off Jeff Suppan. Pedro Martínez started, and in the bottom of the first, he allowed the Cardinals to load the bases with one out. Edmonds hit a fly ball to left field, caught by Ramírez on the run, who threw to Varitek at home plate to tag out Walker attempting to score from third. In the bottom of the third, with two runners on base and no one out, Walker hit a ground ball to first, and third base coach José Oquendo signaled to Suppan to run to home. Suppan "suddenly stopped" halfway, forcing Édgar Rentería to return to second. After stepping on first, David Ortiz moved toward Suppan, who turned back to third, and Ortiz threw to Mueller, who tagged Suppan out. After Albert Pujols grounded to Mueller, the inning ended. In the top of the fourth, Trot Nixon hit a single to right, scoring Mueller who had started the rally with a two-out double to left-center. Johnny Damon led off the fifth with a double to right, singles by Orlando Cabrera and Ramírez to right and left respectively scored Damon to make it 3–0. With two out, Mueller singled along the first base line, enabling Cabrera to score for the Red Sox's fourth run. Suppan was replaced by Al Reyes, meaning none of the Cardinals' three starting pitchers finished five innings. Mike Timlin relieved Martinez in the bottom of the eighth, finishing with six strikeouts, three hits allowed, and retiring the last 14 batters. The Cardinals avoided a shutout when Walker hit a home run to center off Foulke in the ninth, but Foulke retired the other three batters to secure the win 4–1. On the same day the Red Sox won Game 3, The Boston Globe's Dan Shaughnessy wrote that as the win brought the Red Sox close to a World Series title, he wondered how many people in New England were thinking about loved ones who had spent their lives rooting for the Red Sox. Country music singer Gretchen Wilson, a lifelong Cardinals fan, performed "The Star-Spangled Banner." Creed's Scott Stapp sang "God Bless America" during the seventh-inning stretch. Barry Bonds and Manny Ramírez received the Hank Aaron Award for the National and American Leagues, respectively. Former Cardinals players Lou Brock and Red Schoendienst threw out ceremonial first pitches with Rashima Manning from the Herbert Hoover Boys & Girls Clubs of America. A lunar eclipse was visible during the game, the first during a World Series game. The game was played on the 18th anniversary of Game 7 of the 1986 World Series, which the Red Sox lost at Shea Stadium despite taking a 3–0 lead into the sixth inning. Damon hit a home run to right field in the first at-bat on a 2–1 count, giving the Red Sox the lead in the first inning for the fourth straight game, which proved to be the game-winning run. Ramírez singled in the third inning to give him a hit in 17 consecutive postseason games. Doubles to right by David Ortiz and to center by Trot Nixon, who narrowly missed a grand slam after swinging on a 3–0 count, scored two more runs to give the Red Sox a three-run lead. Cardinals starter Jason Marquis went six innings and allowed just three runs. Marquis was the only Cardinal pitcher to go past five innings but would be saddled with the loss due to lack of run support. In the top of the eighth, Mueller led off with a single to right and Nixon followed with his third double of the game. Jason Isringhausen came in with the bases loaded and nobody out and finished the inning without allowing a run. Kevin Millar pinch-hit for starting pitcher Derek Lowe during the inning. Lowe pitched seven scoreless innings, allowing just three hits, and was the second Boston starter in as many days to pitch seven scoreless innings. It was the third straight game in which the Red Sox starting pitcher had not allowed an earned run. Red Sox closer Foulke came in to pitch the bottom of the ninth. Pujols led off with a single through Foulke's legs into center field. After Foulke induced Rolen into a fly out and struck out Edmonds, Pujols took second base, but no stolen base due to fielder's indifference. Édgar Rentería hit a ground ball that bounced back to Foulke on the mound. Foulke threw it underhand to Doug Mientkiewicz at first base to end the game. The series win was the Red Sox's first title in 86 years. They were the fourth team to win a World Series without trailing in any game and the seventh to win after being three outs away from elimination. With the win, pitcher Lowe became the first pitcher to win three series-clinching games in a single postseason, having also won Game 3 of the ALDS against the Angels and Game 7 of the ALCS against the Yankees. Although the series was won in St. Louis, 3,000 Red Sox fans were present, and many stayed after the final out to celebrate, including going on the field when the team came out of their dugout with the trophy. Ramírez, named Most Valuable Player of the series, said afterward, "I don't believe in curses, I believe you make your own destination." Kevin Millar said it was important to finish off the Cardinals in four games and not let it go to a fifth given the team's history. The Cardinals' offense struggled in the final three games, with Pujols, Rolen, and Edmonds, the normally fearsome 3-4-5 hitters, going six-for-45 with one RBI. The club batted .190 with a .562 OPS overall. Walker was one of the few exceptions, batting .357 with a 1.366 OPS. His two home runs accounted for the only two home runs hit by the entire Cardinals team. In the 2004 postseason, Walker scored 21 percent (14 of 68) of the Cardinal runs. The 2004 World Series (4–0): Boston Red Sox (A.L.) beat St. Louis Cardinals (N.L.). The series was broadcast by Fox with announcers Joe Buck and Tim McCarver. Jeanne Zelasko covered the pre-game buildup and the presentation of the World Series trophy. An average of 23.1 million people watched Game 1, the highest television ratings for the opening game of a World Series in five years and the highest average since 1996, also the highest rated broadcast on any network in the past ten months. The ratings for the first two games were the highest average since 1996, and the average for the first three games was the highest since 1999. Game 3 had the highest average number of viewers with 24.4 million since 1996 when 28.7 million watched the Braves and Yankees. It was also the Fox network's highest rating for a Game 3 of a World Series ever. Game 4 posted an 18.2 national rating, giving the series an overall average of 15.8, the highest in five years and the average number of viewers of 25.4 million the highest since 1995. In terms of local radio, Joe Castiglione and Jerry Trupiano called the series for WEEI in Boston, while Mike Shannon and Wayne Hagin announced for KMOX in St. Louis. With the win coming eight months after the New England Patriots' victory in Super Bowl XXXVIII, Boston became the first city to have a Super Bowl and World Series winner in the same year since Pittsburgh in 1979. Manny Ramírez won the Hank Aaron Award and, along with Albert Pujols, a Silver Slugger Award, while Gold Glove awards were won by Mike Matheny, Scott Rolen, and Jim Edmonds. Sports Illustrated honored the Red Sox with their Sportsman of the Year award a month later, making them the first professional team to win the award. For pitcher Curt Schilling, it was the second time he had won the award, having shared it with Randy Johnson in 2001. This World Series win continued a history of Boston teams beating St. Louis teams to win championships. Previously, in Super Bowl XXXVI, the Patriots upset the Rams to win their first Super Bowl and herald a dynasty led by Tom Brady and Bill Belichick; the Bruins swept the Blues in the 1970 Stanley Cup Finals (with Game 4 remembered for Bobby Orr's Cup-winning overtime goal); and the Celtics (led by Bill Russell) met the Hawks four times from 1957 to 1961 for the NBA championship and won three times, including the first in a dynasty in 1957. With championship showdowns between teams from Boston and St. Louis seen in Major League Baseball, the NFL, NBA, and NHL, it is the only showdown between teams from two specific locations seen in each of these four leagues. St. Louis would finally end Boston's dominance against them when the Blues defeated the Bruins in the 2019 Stanley Cup Finals. Game 4 is the last World Series game to take place in a multi-purpose stadium, ending the cookie-cutter era of MLB stadiums from the 1960s–1970s.

The Red Sox won the World Series, ending the "Curse of the Bambino" that had affected the team since they sold Babe Ruth to the New York Yankees in 1919. Pitcher Derek Lowe and other players stated that the team would no longer hear "1918!" at Yankee Stadium, and Kevin Millar told fans to rip up those posters, emphasizing the significance of the victory for Boston. Previous Red Sox players, including Johnny Pesky, who had been involved in the 1946 "Mad Dash" incident, were embraced during celebrations as representatives of past teams. This win marked the first time since 1979 that the same city had both a Super Bowl and World Series champion in the same year, following the Patriots' Super Bowl XXXVIII victory in February 2004, and the last such occurrence had been in Pittsburgh in 1980. Boston then won seven championships in the next decade across MLB, NFL, NBA, and NHL, including one in each league after the Patriots won two more Super Bowls, the Celtics won the 2008 NBA title, and the Bruins won the Stanley Cup in 2011. Following the Bruins' 2011 Stanley Cup victory, Boston Globe columnist Dan Shaughnessy ranked all seven championships and selected the Red Sox' 2004 World Series win as the greatest Boston sports achievement during that decade. Red Sox manager Terry Francona became the third manager in four years to win a World Series in his first year, following Bob Brenly of the 2001 Diamondbacks and Jack McKeon of the 2003 Marlins. Massachusetts Senator John Kerry, who was the Democratic presidential nominee that summer, wore a Red Sox cap the day after the series ended and praised the team for overcoming odds and showing what heart is. President George W. Bush made a phone call to congratulate team owners and leaders and later invited the team to the White House, where he asked, "what took [them] so long?" Mitt Romney, then Massachusetts Governor, ceremonially removed the "Reverse the Curse" sign on Storrow Drive. The day after the win, the Boston Globe more than doubled its daily print run to 1.2 million copies with the headline "YES!!!" on the front page. The team held a victory parade on October 30, featuring 17 duck boats with loudspeakers, extended to include the Charles River to accommodate fans, and over three million people attended, making it the largest gathering in Boston's history. The parade began at Fenway Park, moved east on Boylston Street, then west on Tremont Street and Storrow Drive before entering the river, with one lane on Massachusetts Avenue closed for media coverage under the Harvard Bridge. Ramírez held a sign reading "Jeter is playing golf today. This is better!" throughout the parade, echoing a similar moment from the 1980 Phillies victory. The Red Sox received their World Series rings on April 11, 2005, at a ceremony before their first home game of the 2005 season, with former players Bobby Doerr, Dom DiMaggio, Johnny Pesky, and Carl Yastrzemski, as well as the Boston Symphony and Boston Pops Orchestras, in attendance. Five red pennants were unfurled at the Green Monster showing previous World Series wins, and a large banner read "2004 World Series Champions." James Taylor performed "America the Beautiful," and 19 U.S. Army and Marine Corps veterans who served in Iraq walked onto the field. Moments of silence honored Pope John Paul II, who died nine days earlier, and former pitcher Dick Radatz. The rings were handed out by owner John W. Henry, with former players Lowe and Dave Roberts, who had joined the Dodgers and Padres, also present. The ceremony ended with stars from other Boston teams—Celtics' Bill Russell, Bruins' Bobby Orr, Patriots' Tedy Bruschi and Richard Seymour—throwing ceremonial first pitches, highlighting the region's recent success. The Red Sox rivals gave a standing ovation to the team when they entered the visitors' dugout, breaking the tradition of booing opposing players, especially after Mariano Rivera, who had blown saves in Games 4 and 5 of the 2004 ALCS, was introduced and received a mock appreciation from him. The Red Sox also celebrated the 10-year anniversary of their 2004 championship on May 28, 2014, hosting the Atlanta Braves, with Ramirez throwing out the first pitch to Varitek, reversing a previous play where Ramirez had cut off Damon's throw. On April 9, 2024, the team reunited for the 20-year anniversary of the 2004 title, hosting the Baltimore Orioles on Opening Day, with the ceremony honoring the deaths of Wakefield (October 1, 2023), Stacy (February 29, 2024), and Lucchino (April 2, 2024), and Tim and Stacy's children, Trevor and Brianna, leading the 2004 team from left field, with Brianna throwing the first pitch to Varitek. The Cardinals, despite having the best regular season in over 60 years, failed to win a game in the Series, with reporters blaming Rolen, Edmonds, and Reggie Sanders, who combined for one hit in 39 at-bats. This marked the last time Busch Memorial Stadium hosted a World Series, as the Cardinals moved to the new Busch Stadium in their 2006 championship season, their first since 1982. Both teams made the playoffs the following season; the Red Sox lost to the Chicago White Sox in the ALDS, who ended their own "Curse of the Black Sox," and the Cardinals lost to the Houston Astros in a repeat of the previous season's NLCS. Boston saw further success when the Patriots won Super Bowl XXXIX three months after the Red Sox victory, making it the first time since 1980 that a city had two Super Bowl winners and a World Series winner in the same 12-month period. The Cardinals won the 2006 World Series, beating the Detroit Tigers in five games, becoming the first team since the Yankees in 1923 to win a championship in their first season in a new stadium, and Tony La Russa became the only manager to win World Series titles in both leagues, continuing to wear number 10 in tribute to Sparky Anderson. The Red Sox won the World Series the following year, sweeping the Colorado Rockies. Tom Werner and Larry Lucchino stated that the 2004 title was for parents and grandparents who endured the Curse of the Bambino, while the 2007 title was for children, grandchildren, and Red Sox Nation. The Red Sox met the Cardinals again in the 2013 World Series, winning in six games—the first time Boston had clinched a World Series at home since 1918—and won another title in 2018, defeating the Los Angeles Dodgers 4 games to 1. Twelve years later, the Chicago Cubs ended their 108-year championship drought by defeating the Cleveland Indians in seven games, with Theo Epstein credited for helping end two major curses in sports. The losing manager in that Series was Terry Francona, who had led the Red Sox to both the 2004 and 2007 championships, while the winning manager, Joe Maddon, like La Russa, had managed pennant-winning teams in both leagues, having previously managed the 2008 Tampa Bay Rays. In the 2021 NLDS, 2004 Red Sox members faced each other as managers, with Dave Roberts' Dodgers defeating Gabe Kapler's Giants in five games. Four years later, Terry Francona, managing the Cincinnati Reds, lost to Roberts' Dodgers in the 2025 NL Wild Card Series.
